answer.summary: Moesta recommends a concise, Pixar-inspired sequence that shows your core skills, what changed, the journey that followed, and where you want to go—so the listener can understand and feel that journey.

sections.heading: Practical structure
sections.content: Use a short, roughly six- or seven-statement, elevator-pitch-style story: “Once upon a time” establishes your starting point; “every day” describes your recurring strengths or core skills; “one day” names the change or realization; then use “because of that” to link the next steps in your journey, ending with what you ultimately built or where you want to go. Moesta frames it as writing the script for yourself and stresses distilling it so it is concise.

sections.heading: What the story should help the listener understand
sections.content: It should make clear what your core skills are, why you changed, and how your experiences led toward your future direction. The concise telling should intrigue the listener to ask follow-up questions and help them both see and feel the journey you are trying to take.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately describes Moesta’s Pixar-inspired structure: establish a starting point, cover core skills, identify a turning point, connect the journey with “because of that,” and show where it leads. It also captures his advice to keep the story concise and engaging so listeners can follow and understand the direction of the journey. These points are supported by S1 and S2, and no unsupported claim of missing information is made.
